idea-plugin.name: Reclazz
idea-plugin.description:
Hot-Reload for SAP Commerce and Spring, Free and Open Source

Edit your Java code, build, and the running JVM picks up the change in about 50ms. No server restart, and the application state you spent five minutes setting up survives. Write a new Spring MVC endpoint and it answers on the next request, which is the moment a reload is worth the most.

Built for SAP Commerce (Hybris), where the restart hurts most. Save a *-items.xml or *-beans.xml and Reclazz runs the platform's own code generation in the background and reloads the regenerated model and DTO classes, instead of ant clean all and a restart. Reloading Java is only half of a hybris day, so the rest is covered too: a property is applied to the running server, a locales file re-reads the text behind type and enum names, backoffice labels refresh, interceptors re-register and ImpEx can auto-import. The agent installs through the platform's documented append properties, so it survives ant clean all rather than being wiped by it.

It works just as well on any Spring Boot application, and on plain Java through a watch directory.

SAP Commerce

  • items.xml and beans.xml: regeneration plus reload of the model and DTO classes, without the full rebuild. A new attribute still needs a database column, so Reclazz reminds you to run Update Running System rather than touching your database itself
  • Properties: saving a property file applies the keys whose value differs to the running server, the same call the HAC console makes, and says which values still need a restart instead of reporting them as done
  • Log levels: SAP Commerce keeps them in the property files rather than a log4j2.xml, as a name and level pair. Change one and it reaches the running Log4j2 context, so turning a class up to debug costs a save instead of a restart
  • Type and enum text: editing a locales file re-reads the platform's localization cache, so the new text is served on the next lookup, with no system update and no database write
  • Backoffice labels: label files reach the cache backoffice actually reads from, every copy of it; reopen the view and the text is there
  • Interceptor reload: Validate, Prepare, Load and Remove interceptors re-register
  • Backoffice configuration: saving a *-backoffice-config.xml resets cockpit's own configuration caches through its Resettable contract, so the next view open re-reads it (never resetToDefaults, which would erase what users customised in the running backoffice)
  • ImpEx auto-import: changed .impex files can be imported on save (opt-in), and one carrying a REMOVE header is refused rather than run against your database
  • Extension-aware: understands the extension layout, classpath and classloader hierarchy, and covers every live application context rather than only the root one

Spring

  • Bean refresh: singletons are destroyed and recreated, and references still holding the old instance are re-pointed at the new one
  • New bean classes: a brand-new @Service, @Component or @RestController file becomes a live bean on any JDK 17+, its constructor autowired and its mappings served on the next request, instead of waiting for the next restart's component scan
  • Security rules: an edited @EnableWebSecurity configuration is rebuilt into the running filter chain, so a route that was permitAll starts answering 401 without a restart. Method security (@PreAuthorize, @Secured and friends) is re-read on the service class that carries it, not only on the security configuration: the resolved-once metadata is cleared and refilled from fresh Method objects, because the one the proxy carries would keep answering with the rule it read at startup
  • Annotation metadata: an edited @Transactional or @Cacheable takes effect, not just the body it sits on: the parsed metadata Spring files under the method is re-read
  • MVC re-scan: mappings are re-registered when a controller changes, and an endpoint you add is served on the next request instead of after a restart
  • Cache eviction: caches for @Cacheable and @CacheEvict classes are evicted
  • Scheduler and events: @Scheduled tasks and @EventListener methods are re-registered
  • AOP, @Async and Spring Data: proxy caches cleared, beans re-processed, repositories refreshed
  • JPA entities: the entity class reloads and the Hibernate second-level cache is evicted. A field you add to an entity is picked up by the mapping when you opt in with jpaRefresh=true, on JetBrains Runtime or DCEVM with ddl-auto at update, create or create-drop: Reclazz rebuilds the persistence unit, the schema action creates the column, and repositories injected before the rebuild keep working. In every other configuration it names the field, says it is neither saved nor loaded, and reads your ddl-auto to tell you whether a restart is enough or the column has to exist first, instead of leaving you hunting for why the value comes back null. A brand-new @Entity class is different and better: it is entirely real, so with the same opt-in it is added to the persistence unit and mapped on any JDK 17+
  • Property and logging changes: a changed key goes into the running Environment and the @ConfigurationProperties beans that read it are rebound, so a timeout or a feature flag applies on the next call. Levels, and a saved logback.xml or log4j2.xml, reach the running logging context. A bean bound through its constructor (a record) is replaced rather than mutated, a @Value field is re-resolved in place, and a bean that takes a changed @Value through its constructor is rebuilt the same way; a SpEL @Value is the one left waiting, and Reclazz says so instead of reporting it as applied
  • Message bundles: a saved messages.properties drops the message source's cache, and the JDK ResourceBundle cache underneath it, so the next lookup reads the file
  • Templates: editing a Thymeleaf or Freemarker template takes effect on the next render, without a restart and without turning caching off.

The engine

  • Structural changes on a stock JDK: add and remove methods and instance fields, and change annotations, on any JDK 17+. No patched JVM required. An added instance field is set on objects created after the reload. An added static field gets its initial value too: a compile-time constant is read from the field itself, and an initialiser that stands on its own is lifted out of the class initialiser and run, so a static block with side effects is never re-executed. Where the two cannot be separated the field reads as null or 0 and Reclazz names it and says why. An enum value added on the end is applied to the running JVM on JDK 17 through 25: values(), valueOf(), switches and the EnumMap/EnumSet built before the reload all see it. Adding a constant means writing a final field, which needs an access JDK 26 refuses by default; there Reclazz falls back to the JDK's own jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe, which that deprecation does not cover, so the feature outlives the schedule instead of ending on it, and --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow is a way to keep it quiet rather than the only way to keep it working. A value removed from the END goes too, because the tail moves no ordinal and every survivor keeps its number. Inserting or reordering values renumbers every ordinal after the change, including any @Enumerated column already in your database, so that is refused with an explanation rather than half-applied. A member you delete stops being visible to reflection, so a removed getter is no longer serialised into responses by a framework that never knew it was gone, while code that already holds it keeps running the implementation it had: one outcome rather than three, and never a live request made to throw for a removal you made on purpose. A lambda written into a method you edit links and runs, which on a stock JDK it did not. And a changed compile-time constant is named together with the files that inlined it: javac leaves no reference at a use site, so the changed class cannot reach them, but the sources that read it can be found and are listed, and with autoCompile they are rebuilt and hot-swapped so the new value is live. JetBrains Runtime or DCEVM additionally makes new members visible to reflection, and applies an added or removed interface to the loaded class, objects created before the reload included. A changed superclass is refused by every JVM, JBR included; the method bodies you edited in the same save are still applied and the log tells you the class keeps its old superclass until a restart, instead of losing that work too
  • Instant: classes are redefined through the Instrumentation API in milliseconds
  • One click setup: once enabled, the agent is injected into your run configurations for you
  • It explains itself: when nothing happens, ask why. The build did not reach the class, it is built somewhere Reclazz does not watch, the bytes came out identical, or the JVM has not loaded it yet; none of those produce an error, which is why the log was empty. A second question lists what this session did that a restart would still change, and says so plainly when there is nothing
  • 100% local and private: no telemetry, no analytics, no outbound network requests. The one socket it opens is bound to loopback

How It Works

  1. Reclazz asks once whether to turn on. It ships switched off, because enabling it puts an agent into the JVM that runs your code
  2. Run your application. The agent is injected automatically (SAP Commerce servers start outside the IDE, so Reclazz offers to install it into the platform properties instead)
  3. Edit code, build your project. Changes are hot-swapped instantly

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2023.3+
  • JDK 17+
  • SAP Commerce 2211 or later for the Hybris-specific features, including the 2211-jdk21 line (Java 21 and Spring 6.2) that every installation has to be on to keep building after 31 August 2026; that is the line the 23 integration scenarios run against

idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.28

  • Method security is re-read on reload. @PreAuthorize is resolved once per method and filed under a key a redefinition does not change, so an edited rule kept being enforced as written; and a rule edited on a service never reached the security path at all, because a service is not a security configuration. Both halves fixed and measured on a live Boot 3.3 server, in both directions, @Secured and JSR-250 included
  • A bean that takes a changed @Value through its constructor is rebuilt, the same answer a constructor-bound @ConfigurationProperties record already had. A constructor parameter has no field to write into, so the instance is replaced and its holders re-pointed
  • The sources that inlined a changed compile-time constant are found and named, and rebuilt where Reclazz is the compiler. javac leaves no reference at a use site, so the changed class cannot reach them; the project can, because they are the sources that read it. A constants-only holder is covered too, though the JVM never loads it
  • A removed method's callers keep the implementation they had. The same edit used to do three different things depending on history nobody can see, and the worst of them threw UnsupportedOperationException on a live request for a removal you made on purpose
  • Enum appends survive JDK 26. What JEP 471 closes is sun.misc.Unsafe; the JDK's own Unsafe does the same writes, is not deprecated, and is not governed by that flag. Reclazz opens it with the agent's own module access, so the flag is now a way to keep this quiet rather than the only way to keep it working
  • A saved messages.properties is re-read outside SAP Commerce: the message source's cache is dropped, and the JDK ResourceBundle cache underneath it, so the next lookup reads the file
  • A constructor the JVM will not redefine is said out loud when it costs a value. Once a class carries members added since startup, a field added by a later save reads its default even on objects created after the reload; that went to a verbose-only line and now names the fields and the reason
  • 541 unit tests, and 21 of 23 integration scenarios on a live SAP Commerce server, which is where the suite was before this work

1.0.27

  • A brand-new class becomes a live bean. Component scanning runs once at startup, so a @Service or @RestController you create afterwards used to exist only after a restart. It now registers and wires itself on any JDK 17+, constructor injection included, and a new controller's mappings answer on the next request
  • A brand-new @Entity is mapped without a restart, on any JDK 17+ with jpaRefresh=true: a fresh class is entirely real, so Reclazz adds it to the persistence unit and rebuilds (44 ms measured), and ddl-auto at update or create makes its table
  • Spring Security rules reach the running filter chain. An edited @EnableWebSecurity configuration is rebuilt and swapped in, so a route that was permitAll answers 401 on the next request. Method security (@PreAuthorize) keeps its own metadata and is named as still needing a restart
  • An edited @Transactional or @Cacheable takes effect, not just the body it sits on. Spring files the parsed metadata under the method, which a redefinition does not change, so a flipped readOnly kept running read-only and a disabling condition kept caching, with nothing reporting it
  • A lambda written into a method you edit links and runs. On a stock JDK both halves of javac's lambda encoding broke, and the first call threw NoSuchMethodError out of a line that looked ordinary
  • Immutable configuration picks up property changes. A constructor-bound @ConfigurationProperties record is rebuilt against the updated Environment and its holders re-pointed; a @Value field is re-resolved in place
  • Members you delete stop being visible to reflection, so a removed getter is no longer serialised into responses by a framework that never knew it was gone
  • The last enum value can be removed as well as added: the tail moves no ordinal, so every survivor keeps its number
  • A changed compile-time constant is named. javac inlined the old value into every other class, and no tool can reach those from the class that changed; saying so beats letting you find it
  • SAP Commerce: saving a *-backoffice-config.xml resets cockpit's own configuration caches. And the JPA mapping refresh finally has a settings checkbox instead of only an agent argument
  • An internal audit closed two classloader leaks and bounded a cache that grew with the size of the codebase. The integration suite is now 23 scenarios, all green on a live SAP Commerce server

1.0.26

  • JPA mapping picks up a new field, opt-in. Start the agent with jpaRefresh=true and, on JetBrains Runtime or DCEVM with ddl-auto at update/create/create-drop, adding a field to an @Entity rebuilds the persistence unit (65 ms measured on the demo app), the schema action creates the column, and repositories injected before the rebuild keep working. In every other configuration Reclazz names the field, says whether it is saved or loaded, and reads your ddl-auto to tell you if a restart is enough or the column has to exist first
  • A save that changes the superclass no longer loses the whole change. When one method body needs the new superclass, that method is pinned to its previous body and the rest of the save is applied, instead of refusing everything; the log names what was pinned and why
  • An appended enum constant round-trips through Jackson without a restart. After a successful append the agent flushes each Spring-registered ObjectMapper's enum caches reflectively, so serialising and deserialising the new constant stop answering HTTP 500/400. Reclazz gains no Jackson dependency, and an application without Jackson is measurably untouched
  • Injected members are hidden at the root of reflection, not only at call sites, so a framework scan can no longer see Reclazz's own fields and methods
  • Smaller memory footprint on large installs. A classloader leak in the reflection filter and another in added-static storage are closed, and the last-known-good bytecode cache is now bounded (was about 20 MB on a large SAP Commerce install). None of it changes what a reload does
  • On JDK 26 the plugin writes --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow where it writes JVM options, gated on the real version of the JVM that will start, so enum appends keep working; it is never written for a launcher too old to accept it

1.0.25

  • The agent is 0.7 MB instead of 10.2 MB. It was carrying Byte Buddy to generate two probe classes, and in one file only for the copy of ASM bundled inside it. The agent is loaded into the JVM that runs your application, so every library inside it is a library inside your application; this was 25 MB of classes to save sixty lines of ours
  • Reloading starts working sooner. The file watcher used to sleep for a fixed thirty seconds before arming. It now starts when your application reports ready and keeps the delay only as a cap: measured at 4.2 seconds on Spring Boot and 4.6 on SAP Commerce, so the first save after a restart is picked up almost half a minute earlier
  • A class the JVM has never loaded is no longer reported as having been "loaded before Reclazz could instrument it". That sentence was appearing every time you compiled a new file beside a changed one, describing a startup-ordering problem you did not have
  • Two integration scenarios were checking an old endpoint and calling a newly added one "invisible", which stopped being true when handler methods added by a reload started being mapped. The suite no longer under-reports what the plugin does

1.0.24

  • An enum value added on the end now works without a restart, on any JDK 17+. values(), valueOf(), switches compiled before it existed, and the EnumMap/EnumSet built before the reload all see it. Inserting, removing or reordering values renumbers every ordinal after the change, including any @Enumerated column already in your database, so that is refused with an explanation instead of half-applied
  • An added static field gets its initial value. A compile-time constant is read from the field itself; an initialiser that stands on its own is lifted out of the class initialiser and run, so a static block with side effects is never re-executed. Where the two cannot be separated the field reads as null or 0 and Reclazz names it and says why
  • Adding an interface no longer reports a success that did not happen. Interfaces were never compared, so the method bodies landed, the interface did not, and the log said "Reloaded" while your instanceof stayed false. On JetBrains Runtime or DCEVM the change is applied for real, existing objects included; on a stock JDK the JVM refuses it and Reclazz names the interface
  • A field added to a JPA entity is no longer silently unsaved. Hibernate builds its mapping once at startup, so the class reloads and the value is neither saved nor loaded. Reclazz names the field and reads your ddl-auto to tell you what to do: at update a restart is the whole fix, at validate the column has to exist first or the application will not start
  • Changing a superclass no longer costs the rest of the save. No JVM applies a changed superclass to a loaded class, but the method bodies you edited alongside it are now applied, and the log says the class keeps its old superclass until a restart
  • A structural change that carried its own explanation no longer prints the word "null" underneath it

1.0.23

  • A class built for a newer Java than your server runs is now refused with an explanation naming both versions, instead of being reported as reloaded while the application keeps running the old code. If your module and your server disagree about the Java release, which is easy to miss, you were being told the edit had landed when it had not
  • Verified on Spring Boot 2.7 as well as 3.3, and on Java 17 as well as 21 and JetBrains Runtime 25
  • The download now carries its licence terms and a list of everything inside the agent, for anyone reviewing it on behalf of an employer

1.0.22

  • Reclazz no longer keeps a class, or the classloader that defined it, alive after your application has dropped it. Three pieces of per-class state were held in static maps that outlived what they described, which costs nothing while a class stays loaded and holds an entire redeployed web application when one does not

1.0.21

  • A log level takes effect when you save it. On SAP Commerce the levels live in the property files rather than a log4j2.xml, and those now reach the running logger; on Spring Boot so do logging.level.* and a saved logback.xml or log4j2.xml
  • A changed property is applied to the Spring Boot beans that read it, so a timeout or a feature flag no longer waits for a restart. Beans bound through a constructor cannot take a new value, and Reclazz says so instead of reporting it as applied
  • Tools > Why Didn't My Class Reload? answers the question the log cannot: the build did not reach the class, it is built somewhere Reclazz does not watch, the bytes came out identical, or the JVM has not loaded it yet. None of those produce an error, which is why nothing was in the log
  • Tools > What Still Needs a Restart? lists what this session did that a restart would change, and says so plainly when there is nothing

1.0.20

  • A Spring MVC endpoint you add is served without a restart, on an ordinary JDK as well. Writing a new endpoint is when a reload is worth the most, and it was the last thing that still sent you to restart the server

1.0.19

  • Attaching to a running server reloads again. Classes loaded before Reclazz arrived were being handed back in a shape the JVM refuses, so every swap failed and attaching did nothing at all
  • An application starts on a JVM with enhanced redefinition (JetBrains Runtime, DCEVM). One using Thymeleaf did not start at all, because a class the agent installs only in its own engine's mode was missing
  • On that runtime a handler method added to a controller is mapped without a restart, where it used to answer 404

1.0.18

  • A bean keeps its @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async and aspects while the agent is attached. Calls from another class were reaching past the Spring proxy, so the interception quietly did not run, and after a reload it stayed that way
  • A constructor change reaches newly created objects even when the same reload also removed something. A field added and assigned in the constructor used to come back null
  • An added handler method now says it needs a restart to be mapped, instead of leaving you with a 404 and a log line saying the scan ran

1.0.17

  • Adding a method and calling it from the same class works. The call used to fail at runtime, which on SAP Commerce meant an HTTP 500 from the class you had just edited, while the reload was reported as successful
  • Spring XML reload works on files that declare a namespace such as context: or util:, which on a real project is nearly all of them. Those files used to fail to parse and the reload stopped there

1.0.16

  • SAP Commerce: editing config/local.properties, or a numbered file under config/<env>/props, now reaches the running server. Nothing watched the file you actually edit before this
  • Only the lines you edited are applied. A line you did not touch keeps the value the server has, including paths the platform resolved from a ${...} placeholder at startup and keys a later file overrides
  • A .properties file that is not the platform's configuration, a message bundle for instance, is no longer applied to it
  • Saving a localization file whose text did not change no longer costs the next reader a cache rebuild

1.0.15

  • SAP Commerce: editing a localization file takes effect without a restart. Save a locales file and the type or enum name you changed is served on the next read, with no database write and no system update; backoffice label files refresh the same way, so reopening the view shows the new text

1.0.14

  • SAP Commerce: saving a property file applies the changed keys to the running server, the same way the HAC console does. Only the keys whose value differs are applied, and values consumed once at startup are still called out as needing a restart

1.0.13

  • Thymeleaf and Freemarker templates reload: editing one takes effect on the next render, with caching left on
  • Classes referenced from instrumented bytecode are now instrumented themselves. Frame computation resolved types by loading them, from inside the transform, and a class loaded that way never got the infrastructure it needs to be reloaded. JPA entities were the common case
  • A field added by a reload is set on objects created afterwards, and adding a static field no longer throws NoSuchFieldError
  • Added static fields and new enum values are reported as needing a restart instead of failing quietly

1.0.12

  • Notifications can be dismissed again. A balloon posted while a project was still opening could never start its fade-out timer, so it never faded and its entry could not be removed from the event log
  • The JDK capability message is written to the Reclazz tool window instead of arriving as a balloon; it is context rather than an event. A JDK that cannot hot-reload at all still warns

1.0.11

  • The reload log no longer reports a failure that did not happen: the JVM's expected refusal to refresh constructor bodies on a class that has gained members is recognised rather than shown as a raw exception
  • Reconnecting says what happened instead of only that it was trying, including when no running agent was found
  • The introduction no longer says Reclazz is switched off when it is already on for the project

1.0.10

  • Fixes SAP Commerce OCC: with the agent attached, every OCC response came back an empty 400. Reclazz's own injected members were visible to reflection, so the JAXB context picked them up and failed to build. They are hidden now

1.0.9

  • Switching Reclazz on brings up the tool window straight away instead of after an IDE restart, and the status bar item appears only where Reclazz is enabled and opens the tool window when clicked

1.0.8

  • ImpEx auto-import refuses a file containing a REMOVE header rather than running it against your live database; set impexAllowRemove=true to opt in

1.0.7

  • Updating the plugin now updates the agent your SAP Commerce server loads; it previously kept the one from when the agent was first installed

1.0.6

  • Listing text now leads with SAP Commerce support; no change to the plugin itself

1.0.5

  • Annotation changes now take effect on any JDK 17+, no longer needing JetBrains Runtime or DCEVM: editing a @RequestMapping value moves the endpoint

1.0.4

  • Now installs on IntelliJ IDEA 2023.3 and later, down from 2024.1

1.0.3

  • Contact address now matches the one in SECURITY.md

1.0.2

  • The post-install introduction is a notification instead of a dialog shown while the IDE starts, which held the event thread until it was clicked

1.0.1

Marketplace review fixes. No change to what the plugin does.

  • Looks the plugin up through the public PluginManager API rather than an internal one
  • Guarantees the packaged agent is the shaded jar, which carries the dependencies it loads at startup

1.0.0

First public release.

  • Hot-swaps Java classes into a running JVM: method bodies, and adding or removing methods and fields on any JDK 17+
  • Refreshes Spring beans, re-scans MVC mappings, evicts caches, re-registers scheduled tasks and event listeners
  • Purpose-built SAP Commerce support: extension-aware watching, interceptor reload, ImpEx auto-import, items.xml and beans.xml regeneration
  • Validated end to end against a live SAP Commerce 2211 server
